content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn is a type of corn kernel that expands and puffs when heated, creating light, crunchy pieces. It can be prepared in a microwave, on the stovetop in a kettle, or with a dedicated popcorn machine. Popcorn is commonly enjoyed as a snack while watching movies, at sporting events, or as a light bite.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is the only corn variety whose kernels explode when heated due to the moisture trapped inside.
The first commercial popcorn machine was invented in the United States in 1885.
In the U.S., popcorn is a national snack: more than 13 billion servings are consumed each year.
Popcorn can be ready in 2–3 minutes in a microwave, 5–7 minutes on the stovetop, and 1–2 minutes in a popcorn machine.
There are sweet, salty, caramel, and even spicy versions of popcorn.

items.title: Low in calories when prepared plain
items.content: Air‑popped popcorn without added oil or sugar contains about 30 kcal per gram, making it a lighter alternative to many snack foods.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols in popcorn help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3, and B6 are involved in metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Popcorn is naturally gluten‑free, suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: High salt or sugar content
items.content: Popcorn flavored with large amounts of salt, sugar, or caramel can contribute to high blood pressure and weight gain.

items.title: Burn hazard
items.content: Hot popcorn and steam from the microwave can cause burns, so let it cool briefly before serving.

items.title: Additive concerns
items.content: Some pre‑flavored mixes contain artificial flavors and preservatives that may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Hard kernels
items.content: Unpopped or partially popped kernels can be very hard and pose a risk to teeth.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: For microwave use a pre‑packaged bag or a microwave‑safe bowl, following the package directions (usually 2–3 minutes). On the stovetop, heat a small amount of oil, add ½ cup of kernels, cover, and shake until popping slows (5–7 minutes). In a popcorn machine, load the kernels into the designated chamber and turn it on—ready in 1–2 minutes. After popping, season with salt, spices, cheese powder, or caramel to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry popcorn kernels in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Prepared popcorn is best kept in a sealed container for 2–3 days to retain crispness. Discard kernels that develop a rancid, sour, or moldy smell.
